alt: The definition of fracking split into three parts, each explained: the extraction of natural gas or petroleum (a fossil fuel, not a new resource), from shale rock (impermeable sedimentary rock), by hydraulic fracturing (cracking rock with liquid under pressure).
caption: Extraction of gas or oil, from shale, by hydraulic fracturing: all three parts earn the mark.

after: ## Why shale needs to be fractured
alt: Cross-section of rock layers. A conventional well taps gas and oil that moved up long ago into permeable rock beneath a cap rock, and the fuel flows out on its own. A well into the impermeable shale below reaches gas held in tiny unconnected pores, so very little flows.
caption: Shale is impermeable, so its gas cannot reach a well until the rock is cracked.

alt: Two columns. Benefits: energy security, jobs and income, lower prices, lower emissions than coal, existing networks and new reserves, mostly tagged national. Limitations: induced earthquakes, ground water contamination, heavy water use, wastewater, methane leakage, continued fossil fuel use and local disruption, mostly tagged local.
caption: Many benefits are national; many limitations fall on the local area.

alt: Five rows link a step of the fracking process to the limitation it causes and a way to reduce it: drilling and sealing to ground water contamination, controlled by well laws and testing; high-pressure fracturing to induced earthquakes, controlled by monitoring; fluid to heavy water use; flowback to wastewater and methane leaks, controlled by treatment and leak repair; the well pad to local disruption, reduced by siting wells away from homes and habitats.
caption: Each limitation comes from a step in the process, and each can be reduced but not removed.

after: ## Worked example 1: putting the water use in context
alt: Six wells each needing 15,000 m³ of water add up to 90,000 m³. A grid of 36 squares shows this equals 36 days of a town’s supply at 2,500 m³ a day.
caption: Turn a general point into evidence: 90,000 m³ is 36 days of the town’s water.

after: ## Worked example 2: a full discuss answer
alt: Three stacked steps for a discuss answer: benefits linked to the source, such as reducing imports; limitations linked to the source, such as farm wells, a town 2 km away and natural earthquakes; and a judgement weighing national gains against local risks, with conditions.
caption: Both sides, each tied to the source, then a judgement about this site.
